section.title: Navigational Markers
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will list those fairways, harbours and creeks in the United Kingdom which the Royal Navy administers or provides navigational markers where there is no Royal Naval presence or regular naval activity; and if he will set out the policy reasons for retaining these.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: There are four such areas other than those which lie within dockyard ports: the Thames estuary, Benbecula, St Kilda and Cope channel. Markers are maintained in these areas to indicate safe navigation or to mark hazards such as wrecks.

section.title: Solent (Navy Administration)
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will set out those creeks and harbours outside of Portsmouth harbour for which Her Majesty's harbour master has administrative responsibility in the Solent; and if he will set out the policy reasons for the Royal Navy's administration of each of them.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: There are three creeks and harbours in this category: Hillhead harbour, Ryde
95 Harbour and Wootton creek. We are considering whether it remains appropriate for the Queen's harbour master to exercise waterspace management and administration in these areas.

section.title: Dredging
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will list those areas where the Royal Navy or Ministry of Defence procures dredging.
Mr. Archie Hamilton: The three main geographical areas where the Royal Navy procures dredging are as follows:

section.title: Submarines (The Minches)
section.p: Mr. Macdonald: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will list the number and duration of submarine exercises in the Minches since 1985.
Mr. Archie Hamilton: This information is not held centrally and could be obtained only at disproportionate cost and effort.

section.title: Military Bridging System
section.p: Mr. George: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will make a statement on the origins, purpose and state of progress of the bridging for the 1990s military bridging system; which elements of the system will be (a) wheeled or (b) tracked; which equipment it is proposed to replace; how much has been (i) spent and (ii) committed to date; which units, based in which country, will receive the proposed equipment; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Aitken: "Bridging for the 90s" (BR90) is needed to replace in-service bridging as it comes to the end of its planned life. The purpose of BR90 is to enhance the mobility of armoured formations. The system will enable longer bridges to be built faster with less manpower.

BR90 is a modular system. Most of its elements can be launched and recovered by bridge-laying and by wheeled bridge-laying vehicles. Some 60 per cent. of the bridges are intended to be tank launched. The tank launched bridges have completed contractor trials and are now undergoing user trials with a British Army unit. The truck launched system has commenced contractor trials.
BR90 will replace the No 8 and 9 tank bridges and Crusader tank bridge transporters. Some medium girder bridges will also be replaced.
Payments to date total £26.4 million, and a further £7.9 million is committed to the completion of the development phase. We have recently committed £15.3 million to preparation for production.
The BR90 system will be deployed with Royal Engineer units in both Germany and United Kingdom.

section.title: European Fighter Aircraft
section.p: Mr. Menzies Campbell: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence what is his current estimate of the number of European fighter aircraft which will be required by the Royal Air Force.
Mr. Aitken: The current planning assumption is that the RAF will require 250 European fighter aircraft. Final EFA numbers are, however, still subject to study.

section.title: Anti-air Warfare Radar
section.p: Mr. Menzies Campbell: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence when he expects to place an order for an anti-air warfare in-board radar simulator.
Mr. Aitken: Current plans are to place a contract at the end of 1992.

section.title: Air Defence System
section.p: Mr. Menzies Campbell: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence when he expects to place an order for a very short range air defence system for surface ships.

Mr. Aitken: My Department is currently considering a proposal for a collaborative feasibility study with Italy to provide an affordable autonomous ship-borne weapon system for very short range air defence. This would provide protection against future anti-surface ship missiles and would enter service early in the next decade. Subject to satisfactory progress in negotiations, we hope to place a contract for the study early next year, following a competition.

section.title: Attack Helicopters
section.p: Mr. Menzies Campbell: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will outline the programme for the procurement of the attack helicopter.

Mr. Aitken: Later this year we intend to issue to industry a request for proposals for the supply of an attack helicopter. Following assessment of the responses we receive, we intend to place a contract through a prime contractor which would allow the chosen aircraft to enter service with the British Army before the end of the decade.

section.title: Local Area Missile System
section.p: Mr. Menzies Campbell: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if it is the intention of the United Kingdom to withdraw from the multinational programme for the development of the next generation local area missile system.
Mr. Aitken: No Sir.

section.title: HMS Turbulent
section.p: Mr. Menzies Campbell: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will publish the report of the investigation of the fire aboard HMS Turbulent.
Mr. Archie Hamilton: I refer the hon. Gentleman to the answer that I gave to the hon. Member for Plymouth, Devonport (Mr. Jamieson) on 2 June, Official Report, column 540.

section.title: Menwith Hill
section.p: Mrs. Mahon: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence what part of the United States military operates from Menwith hill, north Yorkshire.
Mr. Archie Hamilton: Personnel from all four United States armed services are employed at Menwith hill.
Mrs. Mahon: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence how many people are employed at Menwith hill, north Yorkshire by (a) the National Security Agency and (b) the British Government.
Mr. Archie Hamilton: Currently some 1,200 United States department of defence personnel and 560 United Kingdom nationals are employed at Menwith hill.
Mrs. Mahon: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence (1) if he will make a statement on the past, present and future role of the base at Menwith hill, north Yorkshire;
(2) what is the purpose of the underground operations at Menwith hill, north Yorkshire.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: The United States communications facility at Menwith hill is located on a Ministry of Defence site made available to the United States department of defence. It is an integral part of the world wide department of defence communications network but I am not prepared to comment further on its operational role. It operates with the full knowledge and consent of Her Majesty's Government.

section.title: Vigilante Forces
section.p: Mr. Hain: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will take steps to prevent former British service men from providing military expertise and support for extreme right vigilante forces in South Africa and other countries; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: Officers may require prior approval from the Ministry of Defence before taking up certain business appointments within two years of leaving the armed forces, but it would be impractical, and an undue restriction on the freedom of individuals, to impose wider restrictions on the employment taken up by former service personnel.

section.title: Malawi
section.p: Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what extra provisions Her Majesty's Government have made for drought relief in Malawi.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: Most recently we have allocated £4 million for drought-related activities in Malawi, these funds being derived from those parts of the regular aid which were suspended last month because of Malawi's human rights record. We are considering urgently with the relevant relief agencies and the Malawi authorities how 98 best these funds might be used. This latest allocation is in addition to the 5,000 tonnes of cereals provided earlier this year for Mozambican refugees in Malawi; and the £1 million contribution to the World Food Programme's targeted feeding programme for vulnerable groups among Malawi's own population.
Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will make a statement outlining Her Majesty's Government's current policy on bilateral aid to Malawi.
Mr. Lennox-Boyd: I refer the hon. Lady to the answer I gave the hon. Member for Leeds, West (Mr. Battle) on 20 May, at column 166.

Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will provide details of measures being taken by Her Majesty's Government to monitor the distribution of humanitarian aid in Malawi.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: In accordance with our normal practice, primary responsibility for monitoring humanitarian aid provided by Her Majesty's Government will rest with those international organisations and nongovernmental organisations through which the aid is channelled. Reports on the utilisation of multilateral contributions through the World Food Programme will be made to its governing body, the Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes, in due course.

section.title: Promotion of Democracy
section.p: Mr. Spearing: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will identify the budget authorisation within the current or past expenditure of the European Economic Community concerning the promotion of democracy or democratic systems or institutions; what past and current sums have been or are allocated in ECU at sterling equivalents; where lists of grants made can be obtained; what groups or organisations in the United Kingdom have obtained grants; and for what purposes.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: As a result of the November 1991 Development Council resolution on human rights, democracy and development, the promotion of democracy now forms an integral part of the aid relationship between the EC and developing countries. To consolidate Community action in this area two new budget lines were established in 1991; B7-5052 for the promotion of human rights and democracy in developing countries; and B7-5078 for the support of democratisation in Latin America, both with an allocation of 10 million ecu, about £7 million, for 1992. No projects have yet been fully implemented, but we would expect detailed information about lists of grants and recipients to be made available in due course. A 5 million ecu, £3.5 million, project for support of democracy in eastern Europe—B7-6000—has recently been approved under the PHARE programme.

section.title: Climate Change
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what steps are being taken by his Department to assist countries to (a) assemble stocks of crop plants likely to be more suitable to possible climate changes, (b) review irrigation schemes in the light of climate changes and (c) develop guidance to farmers and village communities on the likely impact of climate change.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: The Overseas Development Administration is funding research to predict the influence of increased atmospheric carbon dioxide on the growth and yield of crops such as sorghum and groundnut. Through contributions to centres in the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research, Britain is a major contributor to the International Board for Plant Genetic Resources. Under its renewable natural resources research strategy the ODA supports research into crop physiology and the development of new species which will be better suited to changing environmental conditions, particularly the environmental stresses of drought and salinity.

The ODA also provides support for genetic resources conservation of crop plants and their wild host relatives at international agricultural research centres and is funding research projects in the Sahel and in the middle east.

The ODA is funding two studies on the impact of climate change for the Governments of Ghana and Kenya. This work includes specialist exploration of the potential effects of climate change on agricultural practices, including irrigation. The studies will present policy options for Governments and will address the institutional means by which these could be implemented, including the need for extension programmes to provide guidance to local communities.

section.title: Air Pollution
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what support is currently given by the Overseas Development Administration to assist with technology transfer for countries seeking regional conventions on the prevention of trans-boundary air pollution.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: No such projects, linked specifically to prospective regional conventions, are being supported currently from bilateral aid funds. We do not have available sufficiently detailed information to indicate whether aid made available through multilateral channels is used for the activities specified.

section.title: Family Planning
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how much money is allocated by his Department towards family planning services; and if he has any plans to increase the allocation.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: Aid programme spending on direct population activities totalled over £26 million in 1991, which represents a 55 per cent. increase over the last two years. Population is a priority in the aid programme, and we hope to continue to increase our bilateral support to population programmes and reproductive health services in Africa and Asia, to the United Nations Population Fund, and to non-governmental organisations active in this area.

section.title: Pollution
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what information he possesses on the financial commitments advocated by the 100 World bank and the International Monetary Fund to ameliorate environmental degradation and pollution in developing countries.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: The "World Development Report 1992", published by the World bank in May on development and the environment has been placed in the Library of the House. Chapter 9 of the report sets out the World bank's broad estimates of the costs for key sectors of implementing policies and programmes for accelerating environmentally responsible development.

The International Monetary Fund provides resources to enable countries pursuing economic reform to cope with balance of payments problems. It does not produce information on the costs of environmental policy measures.

section.title: Local Health Services
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how much money is being allocated by his Department towards (a) the creation of facilities in villages and urban neighbourhoods using paramedical personnel, (b) expanding health outreach support to individual households and (c) encouraging health promotion through localised organisations.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: The Overseas Development Administration spent some £61 million in bilateral health sector assistance in 1990, the latest year for which figures are available. This amount includes support to projects, including non-governmental organisations, active in these three areas, but allocations are not broken down in a form that allows us to identify expenditure in this particular way.

section.title: Aid Targeting
section.p: Ms. Glenda Jackson: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what percentage of Overseas Development Agency funds are targeted (a) through non-governmental organisation projects and (b) through the International Monetary Fund and the World bank.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: In 1990–91, the latest statistics available, Overseas Development Administration funds administered through non-governmental organisations represented 5.2 per cent. of the gross aid programme, and the funds channelled through the International Monetary Fund and the World bank 10.2 per cent. of the gross aid programme.

section.title: Climate Change
section.p: Mr. Dafis: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how much is currently allocated by his Department to protect vulnerable low-lying coastal areas from the possible effects of climate changes.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: The Overseas Development Administration is funding three studies of the impact of climate change, including sea level rise at a total cost of £362,500, three projects on coastal zone management at a cost of £1,850,000 and a research project on the use of artificial reef blocks costing £245,000. The details of these projects are as follows:

tr.td: Study on the impacts of climate change
Study on the impacts of climate change
Preliminary study of Sea Level Rise
Support for the development of coastal management and conservation strategies
Coastal zone management and shrimp culture
Research into the rehabilitation of degraded reefs using artificial reef blocks

section.p: Climate change is one of the key areas for which funding is available for developing countries from the global environment facility—GEF. Britain has committed £40.3 million to the initial funding of the GEF.

section.title: Vietnam
section.p: Mr. Lester: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will consider establishing a know-how fund for Vietnam.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: We have already made provision for a modest technical co-operation programme with Vietnam and have agreed with the Government of Vietnam that the priority for the transfer of know-how under this programme should be the management of economic reform. We are discussing a project that will provide training in this area to four or five key Vietnamese institutions.

section.title: Rain Forests
section.p: Mr. Dalyell: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will make a statement on Her Majesty's Government's policy of promoting the interests of biodiversity in rain forests.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: The ODA publication "Biodiversity and Developing Countries—Issues and Options" explains the priority the ODA gives to promoting biodiversity conservation, including in rain forests. Bilateral aid projects, both on a country to country basis and through British NGOs, are supported. Research is supported through ODA's natural resources programmes including the forestry research programme managed by the Oxford Forestry Institute. The ODA contributes to a variety of multilateral agencies whose programmes also include biodiversity conservation. In addition biodiversity is one of the key areas for which funding to cover certain agreed costs is available for developing countries from the global environment facility. Britain has already committed £40.3 million to the initial financing of the GEF.

section.title: Substances Abuse
section.p: Mr. Donald Anderson: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what discussions have been held between the Government and representatives of the United Kingdom drinks industry relating to
the programme on substance abuse of the World Health Organisation, particularly as it affects alcohol advertising and marketing in third-world countries.
Mr. Lennox-Boyd: No such discussions have been held.

Mr. Donald Anderson: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what has been the British financial contribution to the programme on substance abuse of the World Health Organisation in the current financial year; and what are the projected contributions for the next two years.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: We have contributed £200,000 since the programme was established in September 1990. Our financial contribution in the current financial year has not yet been finalised and projections for subsequent years are not available.

section.title: Kenya
section.p: Mr. Matthew Carrington: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what response Her Majesty's Government have made to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refuges appeal for assistance to refugees in Kenya; and what aid Her Majesty's Government are providing for drought-stricken areas of Kenya.

Mr. Lennox-Boyd: On 5 June my right hon. and noble Friend the Minister for Overseas Development announced a pledge of £1 million to the UNHCR appeal. A further £1 million is being given to WFP and CARE to help supply, transport, distribute and monitor food for 500,000 Kenyans in the most seriously affected districts of northern Kenya.

section.title: Lobsters
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what representations he is making to the EC about the proposals on lobster sizes.

Mr. Curry: With effect from 1 June 1992 the definition of minimum landing size of lobsters was revised to remove ambiguity in the legal text of the relevant EC Regulation in certain of the languages of the Community. The United
103 Kingdom industry was consulted about this change last June and informed of the Council's decision in October 1991. However, in response to very recently expressed concerns we are considering the matter urgently.

section.title: Shellfish
section.p: Mr. Gareth Wardell: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will estimate the number of (a) businesses, (b) employees and (c) self-employed persons who will be affected by the delay in making arrangements for the carrying out of sampling of shellfish in readiness for the necessity to comply with EEC directive 91/492/EEC and 91/493/EEC.
Mr. Curry: I expect to publish a preliminary classification this summer for comment, and to have the classification in operation from 1 January 1993 as required.

section.title: Habitats
section.p: Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what plans he has to introduce new legislation as a result of the provisions relating to the marine environment in the EC habitats directive; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Curry: We are still at an early stage in considering the implementation of the EC Habitats Directive, which was adopted on 21 May. We shall announce proposals in due course.

section.title: Seismic Surveys
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will set out the compensation requirements for oil companies to pay (a) fishermen for (i) fixed gear and (ii) lobster pots and (b) net and line fishermen for damage to gear and for suspension of fishing during seismic surveys.
Mr. Curry: Any payment by oil companies to fishermen whose activities are affected by seismic surveys is entirely a matter for negotiation between the parties concerned.

section.title: Mink
section.p: Mr. Harry Greenway: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what advice his Department gives to establishments, licensed under the Mink (Keeping) Order 1987, on the avoidance of spread of diseases of mink between establishments and to other wild species.

Mr. Soames: There are currently 22 establishments licensed under the Mink (Keeping) Order 1987 to keep mink for fur-bearing purposes in England, and over 38,000 individual mink are kept under these arrangements. In the last 12 months there have been no reports of escapes received by the Ministry. No mink farms currently operate in Wales.

section.title: Sheep Dip
section.p: Mr. Tyler: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food whether the information sought by the Veterinary Products Committee from the manufacturers and distributors of organophosphorous sheep dips 104 includes the results of tests on humans before the products were licensed; whether this data was verified by an independent assessor; and when he expects to publish this information.

Mr. Soames: Section 118 of the Medicines Act 1968 prohibits the disclosure of information received in support of an application for a product licence. However, the Veterinary Products Committee has noted, as part of its current review of sheep dip licences, that certain aspects of the products and conditions of use need further evaluation, including studies of farm operators, including blood tests and details of protective clothing worn as well as studies to show which areas of the bodies of operators are most exposed. The companies concerned have been asked to provide additional data by the end of 1992.
The conclusions of the review will be published once it has been completed.

Mr. Tyler: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will suspend the use of organophosphorous sheep dips and the compulsory sheep scab eradication scheme until the Veterinary Products Committee's evaluation of the health side effects on operators is complete.

Mr. Soames: The independent Veterinary Products Committee (VPC) has recently advised that, at present, there is no clear evidence that licensed organophosphorous sheep dips cause any unacceptable level of health risk to humans when used in accordance with the label instructions. On the basis of this advice I do not propose to suspend the licences for these products.
With regard to the compulsory sheep scab eradication scheme I refer the hon. Member to the reply given to my hon. Friend the Member for Bosworth (Mr. Tredinnick) on 8 June at col. 12.

section.p: Mr. Ron Davies: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will indicate the number of pesticide poisoning incidents involving birds or animals for the years ended 31 March 1990, 1991 and 1992.

section.title: Cereals
section.p: Mr. Quentin Davies: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food whether the revised intervention prices for cereals for 1993–94, 1994–95 and 1995–96 recently decided by the Council of Ministers of £93, £86 and £80, respectively, will apply to feed-quality cereals.

Mr. Curry: The agreement reached by the Council of Ministers on 21 May 1992 included a request to the Commission to submit proposals to the Council on the standard qualities to which prices should apply.

section.title: Irradiated Food
section.p: Mr. William Powell: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what progress has been made on the development of detection tests for irradiated food.

Mr. Gummer: My Department's food science laboratory today published a report in the "Food Analysis" series, a methodology for the detection of irradiated herbs and spices, using a technique called thermoluminescence.

The test has been validated internationally and recently was the subject of a successful collaborative trial in European laboratories co-ordinated by the Community bureau of reference (BCR). A summary of the BCR results appears in the report.

section.title: Seismic Surveys
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will suspend the licence to Elf to undertake a seismic survey until after the summer fishing and yachting season.
Mr. Eggar: I have been asked to reply.

The licensee, now Elf Enterprise (Caledonia) Ltd, was granted a licence in 1991 to explore for and to produce oil and gas lying under block 98-112. No separate licence or permission is needed by the licensee to carry out the seismic survey. The company carried out consultations prior to beginning the survey, and I understand adjusted its plans as a consequence.

section.title: Hotel Inspections
section.p: Mr. John D. Taylor: To ask the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland what inspections of hotels are carried out each year by the Northern Ireland tourist board.

Mr. Atkins: Under the Tourism (Northern Ireland) Order 1992, the board carries out an annual statutory inspection of hotels to ensure that premises meet minimum standards and, as necessary, in response to complaints. In addition, under a voluntary scheme annual inspections are carried out to determine the classification and grading of hotels.

section.title: Teachers (Retirement)
section.p: Mr. Trimble: To ask the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland (1) pursuant to his answer of 2 June, Official Report, columns 440-41 whether he will publish the guidance issued by the education and library boards and the Council for Catholic Maintained Schools relating to the enhancement of pensions of teachers taking early retirement;

(2) whether he will state the number of teachers in controlled schools that each of the education and library boards decided should be permitted to take early retirement and the number of teachers in Catholic maintained schools that the Council for Catholic Maintained Schools decided should be permitted to take early retirement in each of the last three financial years, showing in each case the number that were awarded pension enhancement.
Mr. Hanley: I will arrange for the guidance issued by the education and library boards and the Council for Catholic Schools to be placed in the Library.

For the financial years 1989–90 and 1990–91, the education and library boards and the boards of governors of Catholic maintained schools decided on the number of teachers to be released under the premature retirement scheme in the controlled and Catholic maintained schools respectively; only cases relating to the efficient discharge of the employers' function being subject to Department of Education approval. These same bodies also decided on the level of enhancement.

Under the arrangements introduced in the 1991–92 financial year, decisions on premature retirement, including enhancement, have been taken by the boards of governors of controlled and maintained schools which have fully delegated budgets. In the case of special schools and schools with partially delegated budgets, these decisions have been taken by the education and library boards in respect of the controlled school and by the Council for Catholic Maintained Schools in respect of Catholic maintained schools.

section.title: Rural Areas
section.p: Mr. Trimble: To ask the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, pursuant to his answer of 2 June, Official Report, columns 441-42, if he will state the person or body by whom each member of the Northern Ireland Rural Development Council was first nominated or proposed.

Mr. Hanley: The members of the Rural Development Council for Northern Ireland were nominated by the following bodies: The Department of Agriculture for Northern Ireland nominated Jimmy Armstrong, Pat Jess, John Kelly, Aideen McGinley, Patsy McShane and Malcom Woods. The Council for Nature Conservation and the Countryside nominated Robert Hanna. The Rural Community Network nominated Mark Conway, John Donaghy, Paul McAllister and John McGrady. District Councils nominated John Fee, Warren Loane and Malachy McSparran. The Ulster Farmers' Union nominated Hugh Linehan. The Northern Ireland Agricultural Producers' Association nominated Wilfred Mitchell.

Mr. Trimble: To ask the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, pursuant to his answer of 2 June, Official Report, columns 441-42, (1) if he will list the wards and townlands in addition to those mentioned in his answer in which the Inter-Departmental Committee on Rural Development established that pockets of deprivation existed;

(2) if he will state the other criteria in addition to geographic and social isolation, high unemployment, demographic imbalances, declining services and poor facilities that were used to select the most deprived rural areas for the purpose of the rural development initiative and give the definitions of geographic isolation and social isolation employed by the Inter-Departmental Committee on Rural Development;

(3) if he will state (a) the precise level of unemployment employed by the Inter-Departmental Committee on Rural Development in selecting the most deprived rural areas for
109 the purpose of the rural development initiative and (b) what demographic imbalances and services and facilities were taken into account.

Mr. Hanley: My reply of 2 June, Official Report, columns 441-42, named five main areas which were identified by the Inter-Departmental Committee on Rural Development (IDCRD) as representing concentrations of the most deprived rural areas of Northern Ireland. The IDCRD also agreed that pockets of deprivation could be isolated in most rural areas on a ward or townland basis but that attempts to be too geographically definitive could be unnecessarily restrictive. Accordingly no list of such wards and townlands has been prepared. Rural community groups from outside the primary target areas are not excluded from applying to the Rural Development Council for advice and assistance.

All the criteria used to select the most deprived rural areas can be subsumed within the list included in the question. Geographical isolation was defined on the basis of the absence of car ownership and the close conformity between areas of above average deprivation and the location of marginal or disadvantaged agricultural land.

The principal measure of unemployment was derived from the 1981 census of population and was defined as the percentage of economically active males not in employment. This was used in combination with other measures of deprivation also taken from the census of population to develop an index of multiple deprivation.

In its wide-ranging consultations with rural interests the IDCRD was advised of the problem of the emigration of young people from rural areas and that the elderly were forming an increasing proportion of rural populations. The IDCRD was made aware of limitations of public transport and of high levels of unfit dwellings in rural areas.

section.title: Housing Grants
section.p: Mr. Trimble: To ask the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, pursuant to his answer of 22 May, Official Report, column 286, under what statutory authority the Northern Ireland Housing Executive suspended the statutory scheme for housing grants; and when the scheme will be reinstated.
Mr. Atkins: The chairman of the Housing Executive has advised me that the statutory grants scheme has not been suspended.

It is anticipated that a new renovation grants scheme will be introduced later this year and the executive decided to concentrate its efforts in completing all existing formal detailed applications, to enable processes to be completed before the new scheme comes into operation. In that context, the executive decided not to accept new preliminary applications after 28 February 1992. Applications for special grants and grants dealing with statutory notices such as public health orders continue to be accepted, and from 14 May, the Executive has been prepared again to accept preliminary applications for certain grants relating to the disabled.

section.title: Women Passengers (Safety)
section.p: Mr. Llwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what guidelines are currently provided by his Department to transport planners and providers concerning the provision of public transport which is safer for women passengers.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: No such guidelines have been issued. However, the Department co-sponsored the passenger guidance leaflet published by the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, "Travel Safely by Public Transport". The Department's working group on violence to road passenger transport staff has recommended, among other things, that bus operators install radios and video cameras in their vehicles to protect employees. These measures also help all passengers to travel more safely.

section.title: Vehicle Towing
section.p: Mr. Spearing: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what study he has made of the incidence of accidents on motorways arising from the presence of vehicles being towed by others which are not specifically designed for towing; and under what circumstances it is permissible for such vehicles to enter the motorway system.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: In 1990 there were 32 casualty accidents involving a vehicle towing another vehicle on a motorway. This is approximately 0.5 per cent. of motorway accidents and one in 8,000 of all accidents. Information is not collected on whether the towing vehicle was designed for the purpose.
A vehicle being towed in such a manner constitutes a trailer and as such is prohibited from the right hand lane of three or more lane motorways.

section.title: Distress Watch
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport (1) if he will set out the policy reasons for BT to provide distress watch arrangements on 2182 kHz but not channel 16;
(2) if he will set out the policy reasons for coastguard stations to maintain a continuous listening watch on channel 16 but not on 2182 kHz.

Mr. Norris: Her Majesty's Coastguard keeps watch on VHF channel 16 because not only is it the designated VHF distress channel, it is also the normal calling channel for VHF traffic. It is essential for the Coastguard to monitor and use this channel for them to carry out their functions of maintaining an effective search and rescue organisation. It would make no sense for the distress watch on channel 16 to be separated from Her Majesty's Coastguard's other functions. VHF is used by most fishing and pleasure craft in United Kingdom waters, few of which have MF transmitters. Most radio distress calls requiring immediate response by the Coastguard are made on channel 16. Since 1978 Her Majesty's Coastguard has put in place 120 remote radio sites linked to its 21 rescue centres which are manned 24 hours a day. This is a more comprehensive VHF cover than is now provided by BT.

The distress watch on 500 kHz and 2182 kHz has continued with BT because it has the necessary sites, equipment and, for morse on 500 kHz, trained operators; it would not be worthwhile duplicating these for Her Majesty's Coastguard, especially given the international plan to end the use of 500 kHz as a distress frequency by 1999.
Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what studies he has made of the contribution VHF direct calling could make to a cost reduction in the BT distress watch contract.

Mr. Norris: No such specific studies have been made. Use of VHF digital selective calling (VHF/DSC) would considerably increase the costs of distress watch since much new equipment would be required both at sea and ashore. The cost of this equipment would not be justified by gains in effectiveness.
Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will list the sources of his advice for the review on cost savings on the BT distress watch contract.

Mr. Norris: The review into the cost of the provision of the BT distress watch service is an internal one to be undertaken by the Department's marine emergency organisation, of which HM Coastguard forms an integral part.

section.title: A595
section.p: Mr. Jopling: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will give his latest traffic flow figures, including those for heavy goods vehicles, for the A595 road between Grizebeck service station and Broughton in Furness, together with those between Grizebeck service station and Soutergate.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: Cumbria county council's transport policies and programme document for 1992–93 published in 1991 shows that on the trunk road between Grizebeck service station and Broughton in Furness the annual average daily traffic is 5,500 with 5 per cent. being heavy goods vehicles. Comparable figures for the local road between Grizebeck service station and Soutergate are 4,600 and 8 per cent.

section.title: Clifton Bypass
section.p: Mr. Simpson: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will announce the date upon which the A453 (Clifton bypass) public inquiry is to be held.
Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: The draft orders for the A453 Clifton lane improvement are expected to be published next year and it is likely that public inquiries will then follow early in 1994.

Mr. Simpson: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport whether the terms of reference for the A453 (Clifton bypass) inquiry will include (a) the need for a bypass around the Clifton estate, as opposed to through it, and (b) the wider traffic implications for the Nottingham transport infrastructure.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: The public inquiries will consider all objections made to draft orders published under the Highways Act 1980 together with suggested alternative routes, and will be held by an independent inspector appointed on the nomination of the Lord Chancellor. The inspector, who is responsible for the conduct of the inquiries, will wish to hear all relevant evidence before preparing his report and recommendations for submission to my right hon. Friends the Secretaries of State for the Environment and for Transport.

section.title: M3 Extension
section.p: Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport when he expects to announce the letting of the main contract for construction of the M3 extension: what will be the process whereby tenders are invited; whether he intends to await the outcome of European Commission legal proceedings relating to the environmental impact assessment directive before inviting tenders for the construction contract; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: Preparations for the implementation of this important scheme are proceeding. Tenders have been invited for the main works and are due for return towards the end of August. In accordance with usual practice, an announcement will be made when a contract is let.

section.title: Trans-Pennine Motorways
section.p: Mr. Pike: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what progress has been made in connection with consideration of additional trans-Pennine motorway crossings; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: I hope to be in a position to be able to make a statement shortly about the findings and recommendations of the consultant's report on trans-Pennine road crossings.

section.title: A19
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport when his Department intends to install emergency phones along the length of the A19 through the constituency of Easington.
Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: There are no proposals to install emergency telephones on the Al9 trunk road at present.
Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport when his Department intends to install roadway lighting alongside the section of the A19 which runs through Peterlee.
Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: There are no plans at present to light the section of the A19 at Peterlee.

section.title: Train Doors
section.p: Mr. Redmond: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if the Health and Safety Executive will take action against the current and past chairmen and executive directors of British Rail in respect of causing the deaths of passengers by their neglect in respect of design and maintenance of carriage doors.

Mr. Freeman: The Health and Safety Executive has not yet completed its full report. I expect the Health and Safety Commission to submit the report to the Secretary of State with its advice later in the summer. It is for the executive to consider what further action may be appropriate.

section.title: Heathrow Airport
section.p: Mr. Wilshire: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will publish the projected route of the new motorway spur road that would link the M25 to the proposed fifth terminal at Heathrow airport.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: The possible route of the spur road depends on enhancement of the M25 in this sector. We expect to show the Department's proposals for this to the public shortly. It will then be for British Airports Authority to come forward with proposals for the spur road.

section.title: Aquatic Environment
section.p: Mr. Tyler: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what are the responsibilities and duties of his Department and any agency which reports to his Department in relation to inshore waters, intertidal areas and maritime land; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Norris: I refer the hon. Member to the Government's memorandum on this subject which was submitted to the Environment Committee of this House in the last session. It has now been published by HMSO as part of the Environment Committee's report on Coastal Zone Protection and Planning, Volume II, Minutes of Evidence and Appendices.

section.title: Data Protection
section.p: Mr. Cohen: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will make a statement concerning the privacy implications arising from the commercial use of personal data held by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency and obtained via statute, and the disclosure to police computers of digitised photographs on the driving licence.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: Consideration is being given to the eventual use of the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency's database for commercial purposes. The concerns of individuals receiving third party mail have been recognised. Any decision will take these and the requirements of the Data Protection Act into account.

The police have access to the driver licensing records for law enforcement purposes under the terms of the Road Traffic Act 1988. This removes any data protection restriction on such statutory disclosure. Photographs of drivers will eventually form part of those records and the Data Protection Registrar will be consulted on the implications.

section.title: Fuel Efficiency
section.p: Mr. Martyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what consideration he has given to the introduction of a mandatory minimum fuel efficiency standard for vehicles.
Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: I refer the hon. Member to the answer that I gave to the hon. Member for Halifax (Mrs. Mahon) on 3 June at column 522.

section.title: Bicycles
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what advice he gives to local authorities regarding the provision of secure parking places for cycles.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: Advice on providing secure, safe and convenient cycle parking is contained in Chapter 6 of the Department's Local Transport Note 1/89 (HMSO), "Making Way for Cyclists". This is one in our series of local transport note publications which offer local authorities detailed guidance on providing for cyclists.

section.title: Channel Tunnel
section.p: Sir John Stanley: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport whether he has any plans to alter the route of the channel tunnel rail link as announced by his predecessor last October; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. MacGregor: No. The Government remain committed to their preferred route corridor announced last October, approaching London from the east along the lines proposed by Ove Arup, with a terminus at King's Cross. We have no intention of reconsidering other options rejected at that time. We have asked British Rail to define a route along our preferred corridor and expect firm proposals from them by the end of the year. Once we have considered the British Rail proposals, we will announce a detailed route for public consultation, and a full environmental impact assessment will be undertaken.

section.title: Railway Electrification
section.p: Mr. Madden: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will make a statement concerning current progress of the Leeds/Bradford electrification scheme.

Mr. Freeman: The Government have given the West Yorkshire passenger transport authority credit approvals for the infrastructure. The Government has exceptionally agreed that the West Yorkshire passenger transport executive should acquire the rolling stock by means of an operating lease.

section.title: Rail Services
section.p: Mr. Adley: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will list those services which British Rail may contract out to the private sector under existing legislation, the services which have been so contracted and the services which cannot be contracted out pending amendment to existing legislation.

Mr. Freeman: Under existing legislation, British Rail may contract out to the private sector any of its support services provided that, in so doing, it acts in a financially prudent manner and discharges adequately its statutory duties. BR has already made significant progress in contracting out of such activities, including: all manufacture and some heavy repair of locomotives and rolling stock; all train catering on Network SouthEast and regional railways; Red Star's road collection and delivery service for parcels; design and supply of signalling systems; track weedkilling and reballasting services; train cleaning and station maintenance; and station car park management. BR does not consider that it is empowered to contract out passenger train and track signalling operations under existing legislation, but I have asked BR to consider what further non-core activities might be contracted out.
Mr. Sims: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport to what extent he expects officials of British Rail to consult local authorities about the provision of rail services.

Mr. Freeman: British Rail regularly consults the transport users' consultative committees and, for the London area, the London regional passengers' committee which are the statutory bodies for representing consumer interests.

Where services are supported by a passenger transport executive the level of service is specified by the constituent local authorities of the passenger transport authority. Elsewhere, the extent of consultation between BR and local authorities is for them to agree. However, I understand that BR consults a wide range of interested parties, including local authorities.

section.title: Company Cars
section.p: Mr. Welsh: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what is the aggregate level of subsidy to company car owners for each year since 1979.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle [holding answer 8 June 1992]: The benefit of the private use of a company car is taxed by reference to fixed scale charges. But the value of private use to any particular employee depends on a wide range of factors. Information about these is not available, so it is not possible to provide an estimate of the aggregate extent to which company car owners may be subsidised through the tax treatment of the benefit of a company car.

section.title: Training and Enterprise Councils
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what appointments he has made of chairmen for the training and enterprise councils in Wales; what indication he has given of the length of time to be served by these chairmen; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. David Hunt: I set eligibility criteria for chairmen of training and enterprise councils, but I do not appoint them. The chairmen are elected by their respective boards for periods which they determine.

section.title: Local Plans
section.p: Mr. Gareth Wardell: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales (1) what action he is intending to take against local authorities which have no local plan in place;
(2) if he will publish those local authorities in Wales which have not yet produced local plans.
Mr. Gwilym Jones: The White Paper, "This Common Inheritance", reaffirmed the Government's belief in an effective development plan system and set out proposals for its improvement.

Section 36 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 (as amended) makes preparation of statutory local plans for all areas mandatory and, as indicated in Planning Policy Guidance Note 12 'Development Plans and Strategic Planning Guidance in Wales' (February 1992), my right hon. Friend expects local plan coverage in Wales to be substantially complete within five years.
The new arrangements came into operation on 10 February 1992. No authority has yet completed local plan procedures under the new system.

section.title: Welsh Language
section.p: Mr. Gareth Wardell: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will make available in Welsh the 1992 DES leaflets, "How is Your Child Doing at School", and "A Parent's Guide to Tests and Reports for 7 and 14 year olds".

Sir Wyn Roberts: Separate bilingual booklets for Wales have already been published by the Welsh Office. Parents can obtain copies through schools or directly from the Welsh Office Education Department. I have arranged for copies to be made available to all Members of Parliament in Wales.

section.title: Physiotherapists
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what are the current numbers of physiotherapists in each health authority in Wales; and what steps are being taken to provide training places to increase those numbers.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: The number of physiotherapists employed by health authorities in Wales as at 30 September 1991 was as follows:

Clwyd 127 94.4

Current staffing levels in this and other staff groups in the NHS in Wales are monitored annually under the manpower resource planning exercise which was initiated in 1987. Forecasts are also made of staffing requirements for the next five years. These data are used to inform decisions on funding training activity, etc., within the various professions.

Physiotherapy has been identified as one of four "shortage professions", along with occupational therapy, speech therapy and clinical psychology. Increased training in these professions has been funded through student sponsorships under arrangements which have operated since 1990–91. Over £100,000 has been allocated to train 12 student physiotherapists.

Other initiatives for remedying these shortages are being examined, including possible overseas recruitment. More generally, recruitment and retention considerations also influenced the Government's decision to accept in full the review body's recommendation for an average 6.4 per cent. increase in the pay of professions allied to medicine from I April 1992.
Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what plans he has to consult regularly with bodies representing physiotherapists to discuss matters affecting their profession.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: The Welsh Office enjoys close links with the various professional bodies which represent both physiotherapists and other health care professions. Consultation with these bodies is routinely undertaken as necessary.

section.title: County Council Elections
section.p: Mr. Michael: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales whether he has taken such steps as are necessary to cancel or delay the county council elections due to be held in Wales in 1993 in the light of his proposed reorganisation of local government in Wales.
Mr. David Hunt: I refer the hon. Gentleman to the answer that I gave on 5 June 1992 at col. 662.

section.title: Recycling
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what proposals he has to introduce a ring-fenced credit approved scheme for local authorities in Wales to encourage investment in waste re-cycling schemes.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: We have no proposals to alter the current formula based arrangements for the distribution of local authority capital resources, which are supported by the local authority associations.

section.title: Cardiff Bay Barrage
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what proposals he has for the acquisition of alternative feeding grounds for wading birds displaced by the Cardiff bay barrage proposal; what progress he has made in negotiations; and when he expects a conclusion on (a) taking an option on and (b) acquisition of any such land area.

Mr. David Hunt: My officials are continuing constructive discussions with interested parties, including the Countryside Council for Wales and Royal Society for the Protection of Birds, about measures to compensate for the loss of the existing feeding grounds in Cardiff bay. However, it would be premature to estimate the timing of any land acquisition at this stage.

section.title: Quarrying
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will make it his policy that the strict control applied to sites of special scientific interest, including ancient woodland, will prevent any destruction by quarrying of Carmel woods in the Gwenlais valley, Dyfed.

Mr. David Hunt: Policy on planning controls over sites of special scientific interest was published most recently in Welsh Office circular 1/92. Any application for planning permission affecting the site mentioned must be determined on its own merits in the light of that policy. However, an application for registration of an old mining permission under schedule 2 to the Planning and Compensation Act 1991 is currently being considered by the Minerals Planning Authority.

section.title: Redundancies
section.p: Mr. Barry Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will state for Wales the number of redundancies by standard industrial classification for the latest available year.

Mr. David Hunt: The provisional figures for the period 1 May 1991 to 30 April 1992 are as follows:

section.title: Housing Associations
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what proposals he has for consultation with the chairman of Tai Cymru to set up an advisory panel with representation from appropriate professional bodies, housing associations and tenant and resident associations to regulate the inflation-related annual increases in the level of service charges by Welsh housing associations.
Mr. Gwilym Jones: None.

section.title: Garth Angharad Hospital
section.p: Mr. Llwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what assessment he has made of the impact of the closure of Garth Angharad hospital on the whole of Wales; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Gwilym Jones: Initially, it is for health authorities to assess the implications of individual closure proposals in the light of prevailing circumstances and to consult on any such proposals.
Gwynedd health authority is currently considering the future of Garth Angharad within the local as well as the all-Wales context.

section.title: Training Schemes
section.p: Mr. Llwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many (a) men and (b) women in employment received employment training in Wales in the last year for which figures are available.

Sir Wyn Roberts: Information on numbers of people training under employment training (ET) who have employed status is available on a quarterly basis. The latest information available shows that on 29 March 1992, there were 1,367 people with employed status receiving training under ET in Wales. This information is not collected by gender.
Mr. Llwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will publish the latest available figures showing the average duration of employment training courses for (a) women and (b) men in Wales.

Sir Wyn Roberts: The latest available figures cover the period from July 1990 to June 1991 and show that the average duration of employment training courses in Wales was 29.7 weeks. This information is not collected by gender.

Mr. Barry Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will state, by county and for Wales as a whole, the number of people covered by (a) employment training, (b) the enterprise allowance scheme and (c) the youth training scheme; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. David Hunt: The information is not available in the exact form requested, as it is not collected on a county basis. Figures are compiled by training and enterprise councils (TECs) area, and those for 29 March 1992 are set out in the following table:

section.title: Departmental Responsibilities
section.p: Mr. Dewar: To ask the Secretary of State for National Heritage what responsibilities his Department has that apply in Scotland; and what responsibilities have been transferred to his Department from the Scottish Office.

Mr. Key: The responsibilities of the Secretary of State for National Heritage that apply in Scotland broadly follow the territorial division of responsibilities which existed before the creation of the Department of National Heritage. Responsibilities of the Secretary of State which extend to Scotland include: sponsorship of the national heritage memorial fund; the work of the advisory committee on historic wreck sites; the Great Britain Sports 124 Council and the international promotion of British sport; British Screen Finance; European co-production fund; Audio Visual Eureka; film certification; the UK Film Commission; the MEDIA programme; the national film and television school; the British Film Institute; the work of the reviewing committee on the export of works of art; broadcasting; the British Library and the performing arts. He liaises closely with the Secretary of State for Scotland on these matters where appropriate.
No responsibilities have been transferred to the Department of National Heritage from the Scottish Office.

section.title: National Lottery
section.p: Mr. Alton: To ask the Secretary of State for National Heritage what assessment he has made of the employment implications of a national lottery, particularly in the Greater Liverpool area; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Key: The effect of a national lottery on overall levels of employment is one of the matters which the Government will be considering in the light of the views expressed in response to the White Paper, "A National Lottery, Raising Money for Good Causes", Cm 1861.

section.title: Archaeology
section.p: Mr. Cyril D. Townsend: To ask the Secretary of State for National Heritage whether the effectiveness of the guidance contained in the planning policy guidance note on archaeology and planning—PPG16—which was issued in November 1990 has been reviewed.

Mr. Key: Yes. English Heritage was invited to review the effectiveness of PPG 16 one year after it had been published and commissioned a firm of consultants, Pagoda Projects, to undertake the work. In order to assess the impact of the PPG, consultations were carried out with developers, archaeologists working for or advising planning authorities, archaeologists working for or advising developers and other interested bodies. The report of the review was submitted at the end of January 1992 and a copy has been placed in the Libraries of both Houses.

I am pleased to report that the consultants' main conclusions are encouraging. They indicate that the advice given in PPG 16 has been adopted by every local planning authority in England, and that the archaeological significance of planning applications is now much more fully considered. The PPG is also starting to produce a more consistent approach to archaeology in the planning process. This, and the greater certainty for developers which results from addressing archaeological issues at an early stage, is beneficial both for developers and for the heritage. In the light of the report's findings we are satisfied that the guidance is proving valuable to all parties who may become involved with archaeology and the planning system.

However, the report indicated some matters which need to be kept under review, including ways of bringing the PPG to the attention of smaller developers. My Department and English Heritage will be following these up with the relevant bodies shortly.

section.title: Single Market
section.p: Mr. William Powell: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will list the short title of each of the remaining Acts for which European Community member states must take national implementing measures to implement the completion of the single European market, and in each such case the Community member or members which must still take action.

Mr. Needham: Every six months the Commission produces a comprehensive report for the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament on the implementation of White Paper measures for completing the single market. This shows implementation by each member state. The sixth report covering up to 10 December 1991, published in February 1992, is the latest available; a copy is in the Library—document 4527/92 of 19 December 1991; explanatory memorandum 6 March 1992.

section.title: BCCI
section.p: Mr. Vaz: To ask the President of the Board of Trade, pursuant to his answer of 22 May, Official Report, column 332, if his officials have had any further meetings with the liquidators of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International concerning the convening of a creditors meeting.
Mr. Neil Hamilton: No.

section.title: Renewable Energy
section.p: Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the President of the Board of Trade, pursuant to his answer of 13 May, Official Report, column 138, what matters he is considering regarding the Renewable Energy Advisory Group; when he expects to complete his consideration; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Eggar: My right hon. Friend and I are considering carefully how the work of the group can be best completed. I will announce our decision on this as soon as possible.

section.title: Aquatic Environment
section.p: Mr. Tyler: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what are the responsibilities and duties of his Department and any agency which reports to his Department in relation to inshore waters, intertidal areas and maritime land; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Eggar: I refer the hon. Member to the Government's memorandum on this subject which was submitted to the Environment Select Committee of this House in the last session. It has now been published by HMSO as part of the Environment Committee's report on coastal zone protection and planning, volume II, minutes of evidence and appendices.
Following changes in Departmental responsibilities since the memorandum was written, the responsibilities and duties of the Department of Energy now fall to my Department.

section.title: Coal
section.p: Mr. Gallie: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on the Government's intentions with respect to European Community moves towards a European reference price for coal and its implications for the coal industry.

Mr. Eggar: The Commission has put forward preliminary ideas on reference prices for coal as a device to restrain excessive levels of subsidies for coal mining in some member states. There is no suggestion that the Commission intend to subsidise Community coal production so that it is all sold at a reference price level. We support the Commission's aim of reducing unjustifiable subsidies.
Mr. Gallie: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will list current levels of subsidy given to coal producers within European Community member states.

Mr. Eggar: The amount of subsidy for current coal production in 1990 for relevant European Community member states was as follows:
£ per tonne
Belgium 55.19
France 10.99
Germany 39.23
Spain 18.83
United Kingdom —
Source: European Commission.
European Community policy is to have subsidies for current production by all member states phased out, and the Government fully support this aim.

section.title: Astra Holdings plc
section.p: Mr. Hoyle: To ask the President of the Board of Trade when his Department's report on Astra Holdings plc will be completed; and when he will publish it.

Mr. Neil Hamilton: I cannot say, although the inspectors are well advanced in their inquiries. A decision on publication will be taken when their report has been received and its contents considered. However, it is the normal practice to publish reports on public companies.

section.title: Research
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what was the total research budget of the Department of Energy for each of the past five years; and what is his Department's research budget for the next year on the energy potential of (a) fossil fuels, (b) nuclear fuels and (c) renewable sources of energy.

Mr. Eggar: Total research figures for each of the past five years are as follows:
